subject: biology-hl
topicLabel: D2.3 — Water potential & A2.1 — Origin of cells (Jan unit)

cards.back: Tendency of water to move out of a solution. Measured in kPa; pure water = 0 kPa (the maximum); all solutions are negative.
Always negative; becomes MORE negative as solute concentration rises. In an open beaker Ψp = 0, so Ψw = Ψs.
Wall push-back on the protoplast. Positive in turgid cells; ≈ 0 in plasmolysed cells and open solutions.
Ψw = Ψs + Ψp. Example: Ψs = −500, Ψp = +200 → Ψw = −300 kPa.

cards.front: Which way does net osmosis go?
cards.back: Down the water-potential gradient: from higher (less negative) Ψ to lower (more negative) Ψ — i.e. toward the more concentrated solution.

cards.front: Turgid vs plasmolysed plant cell — pressure potentials?
cards.back: Turgid: Ψp positive (wall pushes back), Ψw rises to 0 → no net movement. Plasmolysed: Ψp ≈ 0, membrane pulls away from the wall.

cards.front: Animal cell in pure water vs in concentrated salt solution?
cards.back: Pure water: swells and can lyse (no wall). Salt solution: crenates/shrinks. Isotonic (≈ same osmolarity): no net movement.

cards.front: How is osmolarity measured in the lab?
cards.back: With an osmometer — freezing-point depression converts to osmolality: more solute particles → lower freezing point.

cards.front: Why does salting meat preserve it?
cards.back: High external solute → very negative external Ψ → water leaves microbial cells by osmosis → they cannot function.

cards.front: Potato-strip osmosis experiment — what does the zero-mass-change point tell you?
cards.back: The isotonic point: external Ψ equals the cell Ψ → no net water movement. Interpolate between data points and quote units (mol/dm³).

cards.front: Cells come only from pre-existing cells — the evidence
cards.back: Pasteur's swan-neck flasks: sterile broth stayed sterile unless exposed to dust. Creates the origins paradox the cell theory can't explain by itself.
Electrical sparks through a reducing atmosphere (H₂, CH₄, NH₃, H₂O) produced amino acids — abiotic synthesis of organic monomers was possible on early Earth.
Mitochondria and chloroplasts originated as prokaryotes engulfed by larger cells — mutually beneficial, then permanent.

cards.front: Four pieces of evidence for endosymbiosis?
cards.back: Double membrane (engulfment + vesicle); own circular DNA; 70S bacterial-style ribosomes; similar size to bacteria + binary fission.

cards.front: What is LUCA and how is it inferred?
cards.back: Last Universal Common Ancestor — inferred from shared biochemistry: same genetic code, ATP, ribosomes, ~20 amino acids across all life.

cards.front: Why are extremophiles relevant to cell origins?
cards.back: They show cells survive harsh conditions (heat, pressure, acidity) hypothesized for early Earth — supports plausible first-cell environments.

cards.front: Order the stages in the origin of cells.
cards.back: Abiotic monomers (Miller–Urey) → polymers → self-replicating molecules (RNA-era) → membranes enclose them → first cells.
Supporting evidence AND the limitation: the events happened ~1.5+ billion years ago and cannot be directly observed — the conclusion is an inference from converging evidence.
Write Ψw = Ψs + Ψp first, then compare against the external Ψ. Pure water = 0 anchors every direction decision.
